Ohne zu sehr ins Detail gehen zu wollen: Die Analysten von Citrini hatten die in den letzten Wochen sehr angesagte Erzählung bedient, wonach der Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz dermaßen viele Menschen den Job kosten wird, dass mangels Nachfrage die Wirtschaft zusammenbricht (siehe Mitte Februar auch schon > Ist da draußen ein KI-Booster im Anmarsch, der den Banken so richtig weh tut?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=90f580e811&e=8f69674dd2>). Good morning Luca,



In the past two years covering fintech, I’ve slowly seen the sector encroach into popular culture.



Fintech sponsors at music festivals are now commonplace, neobank advertising campaigns regularly run across TV and YouTube and celebrity brand partnerships — such as Revolut’s promotion with singer Charli XCX — are becoming increasingly more popular.



But fintech’s biggest pop culture moment thus far can be seen in the latest season of the hit HBO show Industry.



Where earlier installments of Industry centred on young professionals at an investment bank, season four focuses on Tender, a fintech which started out as a payments processor for grey-market sectors — adult entertainment, porn and gambling — but is now pivoting to become a bank.



The show adeptly portrays some of the deep-rooted issues — albeit with dramatic licence — lurking beneath the shiny neon veneer of the fintech industry. Nepotism, fraud and workplaces bereft of personal boundaries take centre stage in the show.



There are also boardroom tussles that lead to the ousting of a cofounder, politicians publicly trumpeting fintech innovation and journalists working in parallel with short sellers to investigate Tender’s dodgy dealings.



But how realistic is Industry’s depiction of European fintech? With the help of industry sources, I deep dived into what the latest series gets right — and wrong — about the sector. People are worried about private credit liquidity

The basic situation is that people work for about 40 years, during which they earn more money than they spend, and then they retire and dont work for about 30 years, during which they spend more money than they earn. [1]  Thats a very broad statement, you could quibble with the numbers, and it is certainly not true of everyone: Some people retire early, some retire late, some die young, some live a long time, etc. [2]  But as a rough statistical average, most people get some decades of saving in the workforce and then some decades of spending in retirement.

But almost nobody will actually achieve that, or probably even want to. But at a level of statistical aggregates, its easier to get things right: Some people will have too much, some people will have too little, but they will cancel each other out and there will be enough money in aggregate. In other words, this problem is one that is natural to address with risk pooling: If everyone saves the same share of their income in the same pot, they can all replace the same share of their working income during retirement, and people who for whatever accidental reason have too much will subsidize the people who for whatever accidental reason have too little.

If all your investors ask for their money back, you will have to sell those data-center loans in an opaque and restricted market, and youll probably get a bad price.

But when you sell private investments to thousands of individual investors, they dont have the actuarial risk pooling that a pension fund has. Some of them are 45 years old, dont plan to retire for 20 years, have plenty of money and really should be able to lock some of it up for seven years  but are they sure? What if they have a medical emergency tomorrow and need their money back? The individual retirement savers have to manage their own risks, so they want liquidity; they dont want to lock up their money the way a big pooled institutional investor would.

And so if you sell private investments to thousands of individual investors, you have to make them some promise like you can get your money back whenever you want. Or perhaps you make a promise like you can get some of your money back sometimes, but the investors hear I can get my money back whenever I want.

As an actuarial matter this isnt that bad, because after all you are doing some pooling: If you raise money from 10,000 individual retirement savers, most of them wont need their money back for 20 years, so you can safely invest 95% of it in long-term private investments and keep 5% to meet a few withdrawal requests.
